memoryText: The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father’s God, and I will exalt him.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Exodus 15:2 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Exodus 15:2 is the first personal confession of faith in the Bible’s story of redemption. It comes from the lips of a freed people standing on the shore of the sea, and it is as true today as it was then.

“The LORD is my strength.” They have just seen what happened when they tried to rely on their own strength in Egypt: nothing. Now they have seen what he can do. Notice the possessive: not “the LORD is strong” but “the LORD is my strength.” The strength of God becomes the strength of his people. When you are weak, as you often are, this is your resource.

“And my song.” This is one of the loveliest phrases in Scripture. God is not only the source of strength but the reason for singing. A person who has been rescued does not just survive. They sing. If you find yourself without a song, one remedy is to remember what he has done.

“And he has become my salvation.” This is the center. The word is yeshuah, the root of the name Jesus. God himself is the salvation. He is not just the one who gives a rescue. He is the rescue. The same is true of Jesus: he does not merely point to a way of salvation. He is the way.

“This is my God, and I will praise him.” Faith is personal. It is not enough to know about God. The goal is to say “my God.” “My father’s God, and I will exalt him.” And faith is generational. The God of the fathers has become the God of the children.

For the Christian, the verse is a daily prayer. In Christ, the LORD is your strength, your song, and your salvation.
weekInReview: This week you saw the exodus completed and the journey to Sinai begun. You read Moses’ song, the first song of redemption, and then watched the people turn to complaining at Marah. You prayed three psalms about the exodus: Psalm 77, where the psalmist remembered the deeds of God in his distress, and Psalm 114, where the earth trembled before the God who brought Israel out. You followed Israel through hunger and the gift of manna, through thirst and water from the rock, and through the battle with Amalek, where Moses’ hands were held up by Aaron and Hur. Then you came to Sinai. You heard God describe Israel as a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, and you read the Ten Commandments, which begin with the words, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” On the doctrinal day, you considered the three uses of the law and how the law relates to the Christian. The week taught that God redeems before he commands, and that the law shows us our need for grace.
reflectionQuestions: Moses sang, “The LORD is my strength and my song.” What is the song you are singing right now? If you are in a season without a song, what would it take to remember what God has done?

How does it change your reading of the Ten Commandments to know that they begin with “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”? How does Christ’s fulfillment of the law affect the way you obey it?
Think of a time when you asked, “Is the LORD among us or not?” How did God answer? Write about how he has shown himself to be present with you, and thank him.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he redeems before he commands.
Thank Christ for fulfilling the law for you.
Rest in him, and ask him to teach you to love his commandments.
